---
title: "Predicting observations the model did not see"
---

Suppose a regression predicts a particular eye-movement measure, such as first-fixation duration, from word length, lexical frequency, and contextual predictability. The distinction among eye-movement measures matters: [first-fixation duration records the first fixation on a word, while gaze duration sums first-pass fixations on that word](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0041766). Small [observed-minus-fitted residuals](../regression-models/residuals.qmd) show that fitted values are close to the responses used to estimate the coefficients. They do not tell us how the complete procedure will predict a response that was unavailable during fitting.

The phrase *unavailable during fitting* must be made precise. A reading-time dataset may contain repeated responses from readers and passages. We could omit one response while retaining other responses from the same reader and passage, omit every response from one reader, or omit every word position in one passage. The need to choose among these separations is the **prediction-unit problem (PUP)**. Each solution to the PUP evaluates a different prediction.

| predictive question | omitted during fitting | represented prediction |
|:--|:--|:--|
| another trial | one response | another response from observed readers and passages |
| a new reader | every response from one reader | responses from a reader absent during fitting |
| a new passage | every position in one passage | responses from a passage absent during fitting |

A random split over rows can evaluate the first question, provided that predictions are allowed to use information learned about the represented readers and passages. It cannot evaluate prediction for an unadapted reader or an unseen passage because other rows from that reader or passage remain available during fitting. This is the predictive version of the distinction between [conditional and population-level predictions](../regression-models/ordinal-mixed-models.qmd#stating-which-groups-are-represented-in-a-prediction).

## Defining the predictive comparison

[What must be new at prediction time](prediction-targets.qmd) identifies which observations or groups must be absent during fitting and what information will be available about them. A [predictive loss](predictive-loss.qmd) assigns a numerical cost to each difference between an observation and its prediction. The aggregation of those losses determines whether readers, passages, or individual rows receive equal weight.

[Prediction bias and prediction variance](bias-variance-tradeoff.qmd) explain why a procedure can follow one training sample closely and still miss new responses. [Training and test data](training-and-test-data.qmd) then separate fitting from evaluation. [Cross-validation](cross-validation.qmd) rotates that separation so that each observation receives a prediction from a fit that did not use it; [leave-one-out cross-validation](leave-one-out-cross-validation.qmd) makes one row the test set at a time, while [grouped cross-validation](grouped-cross-validation.qmd) omits complete speakers, items, passages, or languages.

## Comparing models

Predictive comparison can evaluate a linguistic contrast. A control model might contain design and lexical predictors, while a second model adds a measure of morphosyntactic predictability. [Comparing predictive loss](comparing-predictive-loss.qmd) asks whether the added predictor changes loss on the same held-out observations. The coefficient for morphosyntactic predictability and the change in held-out loss are related, but they are not the same quantity. And neither quantity, by itself, identifies the processing mechanism that produced the eye movements.

[Likelihood-ratio tests](likelihood-ratio-tests.qmd) and [information criteria](information-criteria.qmd) make different comparisons using the fitted likelihood. [PSIS-LOO](psis-loo.qmd) approximates leave-one-out prediction from posterior draws, while [WAIC](waic.qmd) uses a posterior-variance correction to the pointwise fitted predictive density.

[PS2](../assignments/index.qmd) applies grouped cross-validation to reading-time data by withholding complete passages. The passage split, passage-level loss summaries, and interpretation all follow from the target of predicting responses in passages absent during fitting. Thus, the order of this module is deliberate: name the prediction unit, choose the loss, separate fitting from scoring, rotate that separation, and only then compare models.
